passages.title: The Well at the End of the Lane
passages.passage:
In the village of Phu An, where my grandmother grew up, there is a stone well at the end of a narrow lane. Today most houses have taps, and the well is used mainly by the two oldest families, who say the water tastes sweeter than anything that comes through a pipe. Fifty years ago, however, the well was the busiest place in the village.

My grandmother remembers going there twice a day with a wooden pole across her shoulders and a metal bucket hanging from each end. In the dry season the water level dropped so low that children had to lean right over the edge to fill their buckets, and mothers stood behind them holding their shirts. "We never fell in," she laughs, "but not because we were careful. It was because someone was always watching."

The well was also where news travelled. Women waiting their turn talked about weddings, prices at the market and which family had a new baby. If a stranger arrived in Phu An, the whole village knew before he had finished his first bucket. There was no telephone in the village until 1985, but my grandmother says nobody missed it.

Two years ago, the village council suggested filling in the well because the stone wall around it was cracked and a child might get hurt. To everyone's surprise, the strongest protest came not from the old people but from the teenagers. They collected money to repair the wall, painted a wooden cover for it, and now hold a small festival beside it every spring. The water is still cold and clear. My grandmother says that a well is only dangerous when people forget it is there.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A spring festival organised by the village teenagers
How the village of Phu An finally got running water
A village well and the part it has played in village life
The dangers that old wells present to young children
questions.explanation: Every paragraph returns to the well: who uses it now, what it was like fifty years ago, how news spread there and how it was saved. Running water, danger and the festival are details, not the main topic.

questions.q: Why did mothers hold their children's shirts at the well?
options: Because the stone wall around the well had cracked
Because the children were carrying two buckets at the same time
Because the children were pushing each other to get a turn
Because the water was so low that children had to lean over the edge
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that in the dry season the water level dropped so low that children had to lean right over the edge. The cracked wall belongs to a different time, two years ago, in paragraph 4.

questions.q: What does the grandmother mean when she says that nobody missed the telephone?
options: News already travelled fast enough through talk at the well
The villagers did not like speaking to strangers
The villagers could not afford to pay for telephone calls
The telephone arrived in the village earlier than people expected
questions.explanation: The sentence comes at the end of the paragraph about the well being where news travelled, so the point is that the well already did the telephone's job. Money and strangers are not the reason given.

questions.q: The word "protest" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to
options: celebration
objection
suggestion
payment
questions.explanation: The council wanted to fill in the well and the teenagers were against the plan, so the protest is their objection. The celebration and the money came later.

questions.q: In the last sentence, what does "it" refer to?
options: the wall
the festival
the well
the water
questions.explanation: The sentence says a well is only dangerous when people forget it is there, so "it" refers back to the well in the same sentence.

questions.q: The two oldest families in Phu An still take water from the well.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the well is used mainly by the two oldest families, who prefer its taste, so the statement agrees with the passage.

questions.q: The well is more than a hundred years old.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage describes the well fifty years ago and today, but it never says when the well was built, so its age is not given.

passages.title: Thirty-Two Pieces and a Quiet Room
passages.passage:
When Minh joined the chess club at Nguyen Du Secondary School, he expected to spend his Thursday afternoons in silence. He was partly right. Room 204 is the quietest place in the building between four and five o'clock, and the club's only rule, written on a card by the door, is "Think before you touch." What he did not expect was how much he would learn about losing.

The club was started three years ago by Mr Hai, a physics teacher who had never played in a tournament in his life. He simply noticed that a few students were playing chess on their phones during break and thought they might enjoy a real board. Twelve students came to the first meeting. There are now forty-one, and the school has had to buy a second cupboard for the boards and clocks.

Beginners are paired with stronger players for their first month, and the stronger player is not allowed to win quickly. Instead, after every game they must point to the exact move where the beginner went wrong and explain why. "It is easy to beat someone," Mr Hai tells the older members. "It is much harder to show them why they lost." Several members admit that teaching a beginner has improved their own game more than any book.

The club's proudest moment came last April, when a team of four travelled to the district championship. They did not win; in fact, they finished ninth out of fourteen. But Lan, a grade 8 student who had learned the moves only six months earlier, drew her game against the top player from the champion school. Her opponent shook her hand and asked which club she belonged to.

Minh now plays every Thursday and has lost more games than he can count. He says that each defeat comes with a lesson, and that no lesson has ever cost him more than an hour.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why Mr Hai stopped teaching physics to run a club
The dangers of playing chess on a mobile phone
How a school team won the district chess championship
A school chess club and what its members gain from it
questions.explanation: The passage describes how the club began, how it teaches beginners, its trip to the championship and what Minh has learned. The team did not win, and Mr Hai still teaches physics.

questions.q: Why did Mr Hai start the chess club?
options: Twelve students came to him and asked for a club
He had been a tournament player when he was younger
He noticed students playing chess on their phones at break
The school asked every teacher to run an after-school activity
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says he noticed that a few students were playing chess on their phones during break. He had never played in a tournament, and the twelve students came after the club was announced, not before.

questions.q: What must a stronger player do when paired with a beginner?
options: Finish each game as quickly as possible
Explain after each game where the beginner's key mistake was
Lend the beginner books about chess
Allow the beginner to win the first few games
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the stronger player must point to the exact move where the beginner went wrong and explain why. They are not allowed to win quickly, but nothing says they must let the beginner win.

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about Lan's game at the championship?
options: It impressed even the player she was up against
It showed that she had been playing chess for years
It was the only game her team did not lose
It won the championship for her school
questions.explanation: Her opponent, the top player from the champion school, shook her hand and asked which club she belonged to, which shows he was impressed. Lan had learned the moves only six months earlier, and the team finished ninth.

questions.q: The word "drew" in paragraph 4 means that Lan
options: refused to continue playing
lost the game by a very small margin
made a picture of the game afterwards
finished the game with neither player winning
questions.explanation: In games, to draw means to end with no winner. The context makes clear it was a good result against a much stronger player, so it was not a loss.

questions.q: Why does the writer end with the sentence about the cost of a lesson?
options: To remind readers what time the club meets
To complain that the club charges its members too much
To show that Minh sees losing a game as a cheap way to learn
To explain that Minh is planning to leave the club
questions.explanation: The "cost" is time, not money: each lost game takes at most an hour and brings a lesson. This links back to the first paragraph, where Minh learns about losing.

questions.q: Mr Hai had played in chess tournaments before he started the club.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes him as a teacher who had never played in a tournament in his life, so the statement contradicts the passage.

passages.title: Five Days at Bai Xep
passages.passage:
Last summer my family spent five days at Bai Xep, a small fishing village on the central coast. My father chose it because it was cheap and because there was no hotel with a swimming pool. "If you want a pool," he said, "we can stay at home and visit the one near the market." My sister and I were not impressed, and we said so all the way there.

The bus dropped us at the top of a hill, and we carried our bags down a sandy path to a guesthouse with six rooms and one very old dog. There was no air conditioning, only a fan that turned slowly and made a noise like a sleepy bee. On the first night I could not sleep at all. On the second night I slept better than I had for months.

Every morning at six, the fishing boats came back. My sister and I stood on the beach with the village children and watched the men pull the boats onto the sand. One of them, a man named Tam, let us help sort the fish. Small ones went into blue baskets, big ones into red, and anything with too many spines went back into the sea. We did this every day, and on the fourth morning Tam paid us with a squid each, which the guesthouse owner cooked for our lunch.

In the afternoons the beach belonged to us. There were no umbrellas to rent and nobody selling ice cream, so we built things out of driftwood instead. My father read the same book for five days and never finished it. My mother, who normally checks her phone every ten minutes, forgot where she had put it.

On the last day, my sister asked whether we could come back next year. My father looked at me, and I pretended not to hear the question. But I had already decided.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How a family's holiday in a simple village turned out better than expected
The daily work of the fishermen at Bai Xep
Why swimming in the sea is healthier than swimming in a pool
A comparison of different hotels on the central coast
questions.explanation: The children start the holiday unhappy and end it wanting to return; the fishing, the guesthouse and the beach are the stages of that change. The fishermen are only one part of the story.

questions.q: Why did the writer's father choose Bai Xep?
options: Because it had a well-known hotel by the sea
Because it was inexpensive and had no hotel with a pool
Because his children had asked to go there
Because his friend Tam lived in the village
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says he chose it because it was cheap and because there was no hotel with a swimming pool. The children complained about the choice, and Tam is a fisherman they met there.

questions.q: What does the last sentence, "But I had already decided", suggest?
options: The writer was annoyed by his sister's question
The writer did not want to return to Bai Xep
The writer also wanted to come back the next year
The writer had chosen a different place for the next holiday
questions.explanation: The writer pretends not to hear but has already decided; after a paragraph about how much the family enjoyed the beach, the natural reading is that he agrees with his sister without wanting to admit it.

questions.q: The phrase "not impressed" in paragraph 1 means the children were
options: not surprised by the plan
not frightened by the journey
not tired after the journey
not pleased with the plan
questions.explanation: To be impressed is to admire or approve of something. The children did not think the plan was a good one, and said so all the way there.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, what does "this" in "We did this every day" refer to?
options: sorting the fish into baskets
standing on the beach with the village children
eating squid for lunch
watching the boats arrive
questions.explanation: The sentences just before describe sorting fish into blue and red baskets and throwing some back, and Tam paid them for it, so "this" is the sorting work.

questions.q: Every room in the guesthouse had air conditioning.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says there was no air conditioning, only a fan, so the statement contradicts the passage.

questions.q: The writer's mother uses her phone for her job.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says she normally checks her phone every ten minutes, but it never says why or whether it is connected with work, so this is not given.

passages.title: The Twenty-Minute Rule
passages.passage:
For most of grade 8, Ngoc did her homework the same way every evening. She sat at the kitchen table with her phone beside her, opened all her books at once, and started with whichever subject was on top. By ten o'clock she had usually finished, but she often could not remember what she had actually written. Her marks were fine. Her sleep was not.

In September her form teacher, Mrs Lien, ran a short session on study habits. She did not tell the class to work harder. Instead, she asked them to keep a diary for one week and write down, honestly, how many minutes of each homework hour they spent actually working. Ngoc's diary was embarrassing. In one sixty-minute maths session she had counted twenty-two minutes of maths, fourteen minutes of messages, and the rest lost to getting drinks, looking for a pen and staring out of the window.

Mrs Lien's suggestion was simple. Work for twenty minutes with the phone in another room, then take a five-minute break, then start again. Do one subject at a time, and put the others out of sight. Ngoc thought it sounded childish. She tried it anyway, mainly because her friend Phuong had promised to try it too and they wanted to compare results.

The first week was hard. Twenty minutes felt very long when there was nothing to check. But by the third week, Ngoc noticed that she was finishing an hour earlier than before and remembering more of what she had done. The strange part, she says, was that the breaks mattered as much as the work. Knowing a break was coming made it easier not to reach for the phone.

Ngoc still breaks the rule on some evenings. But she now knows exactly how much each broken rule costs her, and she says that knowing is half the habit.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why Ngoc's marks went down during grade 8
How keeping a diary and changing her routine improved Ngoc's homework
Mrs Lien's opinion about mobile phones in schools
A competition between Ngoc and her friend Phuong
questions.explanation: The passage follows Ngoc from her old routine, through the diary and the twenty-minute rule, to the result. Her marks were fine all along, and Phuong is mentioned only once.

questions.q: What did Mrs Lien ask the class to do first?
options: Record how many minutes of each hour they really spent working
Work for twenty minutes without stopping
Do their homework at school instead of at home
Switch off their phones while doing homework
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says she asked them to keep a diary for one week and write down their working minutes honestly. The twenty-minute rule came afterwards, in paragraph 3.

questions.q: Why did Ngoc decide to try Mrs Lien's method?
options: Because her parents had taken her phone away
Because Mrs Lien insisted that everyone must try it
Because her marks had started to fall
Because her friend had agreed to try it as well
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says she tried it mainly because her friend Phuong had promised to try it too so they could compare results. Her marks were fine, and there is no mention of her parents.

questions.q: What can be inferred about Ngoc's homework habits before September?
options: She did her homework in her bedroom
She was the weakest student in her class
She spent less than half of her homework time actually working
She usually failed to finish her homework
questions.explanation: The diary shows twenty-two minutes of real work in a sixty-minute session, which is less than half. She usually finished by ten, worked at the kitchen table, and her marks were fine.

questions.q: The word "childish" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
options: too difficult for a student
suitable only for young children
too expensive to try
dangerous for her health
questions.explanation: Ngoc thought a rule about twenty-minute blocks and breaks was the sort of thing you would tell a small child. It has nothing to do with difficulty or cost.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention that Ngoc still breaks the rule on some evenings?
options: To show that the change is realistic rather than perfect
To criticise Mrs Lien's advice
To explain why Ngoc's marks dropped
To show that the method did not really work
questions.explanation: The sentence is followed by but she now knows exactly how much each broken rule costs her, so the point is that the real gain is awareness, not perfection. Nothing says her marks dropped.

questions.q: Phuong found the method more useful than Ngoc did.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says the two friends wanted to compare results, but it never reports Phuong's results, so this is not given.
